```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4, warning = TRUE, message = TRUE)
library(NationalModelUng2009)
```

## What this workflow provides

This workflow predicts gross merchantable volume in cubic metres per hectare
(m3/ha) using the national models of Ung et al. (2009). Gross merchantable
volume is the volume of live trees larger than 9 cm in diameter at breast
height.

The example starts with a file of stand locations with
their leading species. It ends with one yield curve, from age 0 to 200, for
each species in each stand.

## 1. The stands

The package includes a small made-up file of 10 stands. Each stand has an
identifier, a location (latitude, longitude and elevation in metres) and up to
three species.

```{r stands}
stands <- example_stands
stands
```

## 2. One row per stand and species

Each species in a stand needs to get its own curve. Therefore, convert the
stands table from wide to long, removing empty entries.

```{r stack}
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, species = stands$sp1),
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, species = stands$sp2),
  data.frame(stand_id = stands$stand_id, species = stands$sp3)
)
curves <- curves[!is.na(curves$species), ]
curves <- curves[order(curves$stand_id), ]
curves
```

## 3. Get the climate for each stand

The models need two climate values for each stand:

- `dd0`: degree-days above 0 °C (the yearly sum of daily mean temperatures
  above 0 °C);
- `map`: mean annual precipitation in millimetres.

It is recommended that **averages over multiple years be used** (e.g., climate
normals, such as 1981–2010), and not the values of one year. The models were
fitted with one long-term climate for each plot. Those values describe where a
stand grows, not the weather of a given year.

The package includes options to obtain climate data.

**Option A: climr (in R).** `ung_climate()` uses the climr package. climr
downloads climate maps the first time an area is requested (this can take
several minutes) and keeps them for later use. Some VPNs block its server; if
climr cannot connect, disconnect from the VPN or use Option B.

```{r climate-climr, eval = FALSE}
climate <- ung_climate(lon = stands$lon, lat = stands$lat,
                       elev = stands$elev, id = stands$stand_id)
```

**Option B: ClimateNA (Windows program).** The same function runs a local
copy of ClimateNA when you set `source = "climatena"` and give the path to
the program.

```{r climate-climatena, eval = FALSE}
climate <- ung_climate(lon = stands$lon, lat = stands$lat,
                       elev = stands$elev, id = stands$stand_id,
                       source = "climatena",
                       exe = "C:/ClimateNA_v760/ClimateNA_v7.60.exe")
```

The default for both options above is 1981–2010. For another period, give the
years to average, for example `years = 2010:2019`. This works with both
options.

If you already have `dd0` and `map` from another source, skip this step and
add them to `curves` yourself.

The package includes the results of the ClimateNA option. It is used in this
example.

```{r climate-example}
climate <- example_climate
curves <- merge(curves, climate, by.x = "stand_id", by.y = "id")
curves
```

## 4. Make the yield tables

`ung_yield_table()` makes all the curves in one call. Give it one value of
`species`, `dd0` and `map` per curve, and the ages you want. The `id`
argument labels each curve, here with the stand identifier.

```{r yield-long}
ages <- seq(0, 200, by = 10)
yield <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                         dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                         id = curves$stand_id)
head(yield)
```

The result is in long format: one row per curve and age, with columns `id`,
`species` (the package code, such as `PINU.BAN` for jack pine), `model`, `dd0`,
`map`, `age` and `volume`. Age 0 always has volume 0.

The default model is Nat2 (see "Which model to use" in `?ung_models`).

The warning above is a single summary for the whole call. Here it says that
some curves go beyond the oldest stands in the data used to fit the models.
Step 6 shows which rows are affected.

CBM users may prefer the wide format, with one row per curve and one volume
column per age (`vol_0`, `vol_10`, ...). Add `format = "wide"` to the same
call.

```{r yield-wide}
yield_wide <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                              dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                              id = curves$stand_id, format = "wide",
                              warn = FALSE)
yield_wide[, 1:8]
```

## 5. Add an uncertainty interval

Add `uncertainty = TRUE` to get `lower` and `upper` columns: the range of
volume if `dd0` and `map` were off by about `sd_dd0` and `sd_map`. The package
predicts volume 1000 times, each time drawing `dd0` and `map` at random
(normal distribution, drawn independently) around the values supplied. At
each age, `lower` and `upper` hold the middle 90 % of the 1000 volumes. The
`volume` column is unchanged. `seed` makes the random simulation repeatable.

You must give `sd_dd0` and `sd_map`, the standard deviations of `dd0`
(degree-days) and `map` (mm). climr and ClimateNA give one value per location,
with no standard deviation. Other climate tools, such as BioSIM, can simulate
many replicates of the climate at a location; use the standard deviation
across these replicates. The values below are illustration values only.

```{r yield-uncertainty}
yield_unc <- ung_yield_table(curves$species, age = ages,
                             dd0 = curves$dd0, map = curves$map,
                             id = curves$stand_id,
                             uncertainty = TRUE, sd_dd0 = 100, sd_map = 50,
                             seed = 1, warn = FALSE)
yield_unc[yield_unc$age == 100, c("id", "species", "volume", "lower", "upper")]
```

The interval covers climate only. It does **not** include error in the fitted
parameters, stand-to-stand variation (real stands vary more than the interval
shows), rounding of the parameters, or the model limits (see `ung_check()`).
See `?ung_yield_table` for details.

`plot()` draws the interval as a shaded band around the curve.

```{r plot-uncertainty}
plot(yield_unc[yield_unc$id == "S01", ])
```

## 6. List all cautions with `ung_check()`

`ung_check()` runs every check the package knows about and explains how many
rows each one affects.

```{r checks}
ung_check(yield)
```

The first five checks are the kinds that can trigger the warning in step 4.
The others apply to almost every yield curve, so they are listed here rather
than given as warnings. `ung_check()` always calculates both Nat1 and Nat2,
so it can flag rows the warning did not mention: here, `output_beyond_data`
also counts Nat1 basal area. The limits of 10 years, 15 % and 30 % are rules
of thumb chosen for this package, not values from the paper.

To see which curves and ages are affected, use `rows = TRUE`.

```{r check-rows}
flags <- ung_check(yield, rows = TRUE)
old <- yield[flags$older_than_data, ]
table(old$id, old$species)
```

## 7. Plot the curves

`plot()` draws one line per curve. Here are the three black spruce stands.

```{r plot}
plot(yield[yield$species == "PICE.MAR", ])
```

## 8. Compare Nat1 and Nat2

Nat2 predicts volume directly. Nat1 first predicts dominant height and basal
area `G`, then calculates volume from them. The published Nat1 is biased low;
`nat1_bias_correction = TRUE` adds a correction that closes most of the gap
(see "Why Nat1 volume needs a correction" in `?ung_models`). The correction
was added by this package and is not part of the published model.

```{r compare-models}
s02 <- curves[curves$stand_id == "S02", ]
nat2 <- ung_yield_table(s02$species, age = ages, dd0 = s02$dd0,
                        map = s02$map, warn = FALSE)
nat1 <- ung_yield_table(s02$species, age = ages, dd0 = s02$dd0,
                        map = s02$map, model = "Nat1", warn = FALSE)
nat1_corrected <- ung_yield_table(s02$species, age = ages, dd0 = s02$dd0,
                                  map = s02$map, model = "Nat1",
                                  nat1_bias_correction = TRUE, warn = FALSE)
data.frame(age = nat2$age,
           Nat1 = nat1$volume,
           Nat1_corrected = nat1_corrected$volume,
           Nat2 = nat2$volume)[nat2$age %in% c(40, 80, 120), ]
```

The two Douglas-fir stands show a weakness of Nat2 in dry places. At stand
S10, the Nat2 curve (solid) jumps to about 170 m3/ha by age 10 and then
hardly rises, which is not realistic. This comes from the published Nat2
equation: its climate terms control how fast volume rises with age.
`ung_check()` reports it as `curve_not_rising` (step 6). Nat1 (dashed) rises
gradually, so consider Nat1 for such stands. To draw both models on one plot,
combine the two tables with `rbind()`.

```{r plot-fd}
fd <- curves[curves$species == "Douglas-fir", ]
fd_nat1 <- ung_yield_table(fd$species, age = ages, dd0 = fd$dd0,
                           map = fd$map, id = fd$stand_id, model = "Nat1",
                           nat1_bias_correction = TRUE, warn = FALSE)
plot(rbind(yield[yield$species == "PSEU.MEN", ], fd_nat1))
```

To use Nat1 in a yield table, add `model = "Nat1"` and, usually,
`nat1_bias_correction = TRUE` to `ung_yield_table()`.
## 9. Save the yield tables

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(yield, "yield_long.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(yield_wide, "yield_wide.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Limits of the models

- The authors designed these models for predictions over less than 10 years.
  A curve from age 0 to 200 goes far beyond that; treat it as an illustration
  of the fitted equations, not a forecast for a particular stand.
- The models were fitted to plots measured once, where one species made up at
  least 75 % of the basal area. In a mixed stand, each species' curve
  describes a stand of that species alone. Combining the curves (for example,
  weighting them by each species' share) is up to the user.
- The models have no site-quality input. Two stands with the same species
  and climate get the same curve.
- The climate terms describe how volume differs among locations. They do not
  predict the effect of climate change, so do not use future climate
  projections as inputs.

## Reference

Ung, C.-H., Bernier, P.Y., Guo, X.J. and Lambert, M.-C. 2009. A simple growth
and yield model for assessing changes in standing volume across Canada's
forests. The Forestry Chronicle 85(1): 57–64. <https://doi.org/10.5558/tfc85057-1>
